\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). --- = experiment pending. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok).}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 24.35 & --- & --- & Spike \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.24 & 0.41 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^{*\dagger}$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.38 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 1.94 & --- & --- & Spike \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.

\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$27.3\% PPL.
\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. A single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90) and Llama (0.57, 0.85): no benefit.
\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation; $t_1/t_5$ is irrelevant. Mistral (0.24) and Gemma-2 (0.23): counterproductive.
\end{itemize}

Both conditions are needed: Llama's concentration (0.57) exceeds the 0.50 threshold but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no benefit.
A concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71, Llama at 0.57).
Only Qwen exhibits the spread pattern ($N{=}1$); the suggested thresholds should be treated as illustrative until confirmed on additional architectures.
The rule reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no overhead.

Additional analyses---granularity tradeoff (Appendix~\ref{sec:granularity}), aggressive compression, profiling resolution and stability, per-layer optimality, and KV separation---are in Appendices~\ref{sec:granularity}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

Pythia-1.4B extends the evaluation to MHA (1:1 ratio, 384 heads).
Despite low concentration ($0.24$), Pythia exhibits a spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}1.94$) with sensitivity in mid-layer heads (L1, L8--L17) rather than Layer-0, confirming that the spike/flat distinction generalizes beyond GQA architectures.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent concentration dilution.}
Qwen2.5-14B (GQA 5:1, 384 heads) provides a within-family comparison: concentration drops from 0.61 (7B) to 0.33 (14B), and $t_1/t_5$ rises from 0.57 to 24.35---a transition from spread to spike.
Sensitivity is dominated by a single head (L0H5, $d_h(2){=}1.845$; second-ranked: $0.237$, a $7.8\times$ gap), while the $3.4\times$ increase in head count ($112{\to}384$) dilutes the remaining signal below the concentration threshold.
Spread heterogeneity is thus not an intrinsic property of an architecture family but depends on scale: the diagnostic correctly identifies Qwen-7B as the single model$\times$scale combination where non-uniform allocation helps.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). --- = experiment pending. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok).}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 24.35 & --- & --- & Spike \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.24 & 0.41 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^{*\dagger}$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.38 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 1.94 & --- & --- & Spike \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.

\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$27.3\% PPL.
\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. A single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90) and Llama (0.57, 0.85): no benefit.
\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation; $t_1/t_5$ is irrelevant. Mistral (0.24) and Gemma-2 (0.23): counterproductive.
\end{itemize}

Both conditions are needed: Llama's concentration (0.57) exceeds the 0.50 threshold but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no benefit.
A concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71, Llama at 0.57).
Only Qwen exhibits the spread pattern ($N{=}1$); the suggested thresholds should be treated as illustrative until confirmed on additional architectures.
The rule reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no overhead.

Additional analyses---granularity tradeoff (Appendix~\ref{sec:granularity}), aggressive compression, profiling resolution and stability, per-layer optimality, and KV separation---are in Appendices~\ref{sec:granularity}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

file.content:
Non-uniform per-head KV cache quantization helps only when head sensitivity exhibits a specific distribution shape---a finding obscured by prior work's focus on aggregate metrics.
We study five 7--9B architectures on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ and find that the benefit of per-head allocation depends not on GQA ratio or overall sensitivity magnitude, but on whether heterogeneity is \emph{spread} across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients or concentrated in a single outlier.
On the one spread-pattern model (Qwen2.5-7B), a cardinality-constrained solver achieves 11.23 perplexity at $4\times$ compression---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45)---while unconstrained solvers fail catastrophically (32--37 PPL) due to 2-bit distortion compounding through the residual stream.
On the remaining four models, non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit: Yi-1.5-9B has the highest concentration tested (0.71, exceeding Qwen's 0.61) yet gains nothing, because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth gradient.
The cardinality constraint prevents catastrophic failure on spread architectures, moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: unconstrained $1.47\times$ degradation reduced to within 0.5\% of uniform), and renders solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations---enabling a simple $O(H\log H)$ greedy algorithm.
We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial ones across all five models studied.

+We study seven models spanning 1.4B--14B parameters and five architecture families (MHA through GQA 8:1) on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ and find that the benefit of per-head allocation depends not on GQA ratio or overall sensitivity magnitude, but on whether heterogeneity is \emph{spread} across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients or concentrated in a single outlier.

On the one spread-pattern model (Qwen2.5-7B), a cardinality-constrained solver achieves 11.23 perplexity at $4\times$ compression---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45)---while unconstrained solvers fail catastrophically (32--37 PPL) due to 2-bit distortion compounding through the residual stream.

On the remaining four models, non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit: Yi-1.5-9B has the highest concentration tested (0.71, exceeding Qwen's 0.61) yet gains nothing, because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth gradient.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher, because 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger than 4-bit and compound super-linearly when many heads are quantized simultaneously.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.
The constraint is beneficial even on flat-distribution architectures: on Gemma-2-9B, unconstrained MCKP assigns 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit, producing a moderate $1.47\times$ degradation; the constraint reduces this to within 0.5\% of uniform.

A surprising consequence is that the cardinality constraint renders solver choice irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures (112/112 heads on Qwen, 256/256 on Llama, 255/256 on Mistral), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On Llama-3.1-8B (8.45 vs.\ 8.47), Yi-1.5-9B (7.22 vs.\ 7.22), Mistral-7B-v0.3 (7.16 vs.\ 7.13), and Gemma-2-9B (within 0.5\% of uniform), constrained MCKP provides no meaningful improvement.
The difference traces to the \emph{distribution shape} of head sensitivity, not GQA ratio alone: Qwen's Layer-0 heads form a cluster of high sensitivity across multiple bitwidths (``spread''); Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier (``spike''); Gemma-2 and Mistral show near-uniform sensitivity (``flat'').

This motivates a question prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and distribution shape (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}) that separates the one beneficial case from the four non-beneficial ones.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen's, but its single-outlier spike has no cross-bitwidth gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint serves three roles: preventing catastrophic failure on spread architectures (Qwen: 32.45$\to$11.23), preventing moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: 8.85$\to$within 0.5\% of uniform), and rendering solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all tested architectures (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates the one architecture where non-uniform allocation helps from the four where it does not, across all five models tested. Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher, because 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger than 4-bit and compound super-linearly when many heads are quantized simultaneously.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.
The constraint is beneficial even on flat-distribution architectures: on Gemma-2-9B, unconstrained MCKP assigns 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit, producing a moderate $1.47\times$ degradation; the constraint reduces this to within 0.5\% of uniform.

A surprising consequence is that the cardinality constraint renders solver choice irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures (112/112 heads on Qwen, 256/256 on Llama, 255/256 on Mistral), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On the remaining six models---including Qwen2.5-14B, where the $3.4\times$ increase in head count dilutes spread into spike---constrained MCKP provides no meaningful improvement.
The difference traces to the \emph{distribution shape} of head sensitivity, not GQA ratio or model scale alone: Qwen-7B's Layer-0 heads form a cluster of high sensitivity across multiple bitwidths (``spread''); Yi-1.5 and Qwen-14B have single extreme outliers (``spike''); Gemma-2, Mistral, and Pythia show near-uniform or mid-layer-concentrated sensitivity.

This motivates a question prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and distribution shape (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}) that correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen-7B's, but its single-outlier spike has no cross-bitwidth gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint serves three roles: preventing catastrophic failure on spread architectures (Qwen: 32.45$\to$11.23), preventing moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: 8.85$\to$within 0.5\% of uniform), and rendering solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all tested architectures (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates the one architecture where non-uniform allocation helps from the four where it does not, across all five models tested. Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding.
On Qwen2.5-7B, limiting 2-bit heads to $k{\leq}8$ reduces PPL from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23 ($-$27.3\%) at $4\times$ compression, while making solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures.
Whether non-uniform allocation helps depends on the \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity---spread patterns (Qwen, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$) yield large gains, while spike (Yi-1.5, Llama) and flat (Mistral, Gemma-2) patterns show no benefit.
A joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio correctly separates these cases across all five models, though the spread category rests on $N{=}1$ and requires further validation.
Extending to 70B+ models, integrating with production inference engines, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) are natural next steps.

\section*{Limitations}

The spread category is represented by a single architecture (Qwen2.5-7B); validating on additional high-concentration models is necessary before the decision rule can be applied with high confidence.
We evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); gradient-based or activation-norm alternatives remain unexplored.
We report no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
We have not verified whether these findings transfer to 70B+ scales, and profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding.
On Qwen2.5-7B, limiting 2-bit heads to $k{\leq}8$ reduces PPL from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23 ($-$27.3\%) at $4\times$ compression, while making solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures.
Whether non-uniform allocation helps depends on the \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity---spread patterns (Qwen, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$) yield large gains, while spike (Yi-1.5, Llama) and flat (Mistral, Gemma-2) patterns show no benefit.
A joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio correctly separates these cases across all five models, though the spread category rests on $N{=}1$ and requires further validation.
Extending to 70B+ models, integrating with production inference engines, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) are natural next steps.

\section*{Limitations}

The spread category is represented by a single architecture (Qwen2.5-7B); validating on additional high-concentration models is necessary before the decision rule can be applied with high confidence.
We evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); gradient-based or activation-norm alternatives remain unexplored.
We report no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
We have not verified whether these findings transfer to 70B+ scales, and profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding.
On Qwen2.5-7B, limiting 2-bit heads to $k{\leq}8$ reduces PPL from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23 ($-$27.3\%) at $4\times$ compression, while making solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures.
Whether non-uniform allocation helps depends on the \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity---spread patterns (Qwen-7B, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$) yield large gains, while spike (Yi-1.5, Llama, Qwen-14B, Pythia) and flat (Mistral, Gemma-2) patterns show no benefit.
A joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast where Qwen-14B's spread dilutes into spike; the spread category rests on $N{=}1$ (Qwen-7B) and requires further validation.
Extending to 70B+ models, integrating with production inference engines, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) are natural next steps.

\section*{Limitations}

The spread category is represented by a single architecture$\times$scale combination (Qwen2.5-7B); Qwen-14B's transition to spike under scale suggests spread may be rare, and validating on additional high-concentration models is necessary before the decision rule can be applied with high confidence.
Although we evaluate seven models spanning 1.4B--14B parameters and five architecture families, this is still too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); gradient-based or activation-norm alternatives remain unexplored.
We report no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
We have not verified whether these findings transfer to 70B+ scales, and profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher, because 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger than 4-bit and compound super-linearly when many heads are quantized simultaneously.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.
The constraint is beneficial even on flat-distribution architectures: on Gemma-2-9B, unconstrained MCKP assigns 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit, producing a moderate $1.47\times$ degradation; the constraint reduces this to within 0.5\% of uniform.

A surprising consequence is that the cardinality constraint renders solver choice irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures (112/112 heads on Qwen, 256/256 on Llama, 255/256 on Mistral), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On the remaining six models---including Qwen2.5-14B, where the $3.4\times$ increase in head count dilutes spread into spike---constrained MCKP provides no meaningful improvement.
The difference traces to the \emph{distribution shape} of head sensitivity, not GQA ratio or model scale alone: Qwen-7B's Layer-0 heads form a cluster of high sensitivity across multiple bitwidths (``spread''); Yi-1.5 and Qwen-14B have single extreme outliers (``spike''); Gemma-2, Mistral, and Pythia show near-uniform or mid-layer-concentrated sensitivity.

This motivates a question prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint empirical decision rule based on concentration and distribution shape (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}) that correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen-7B's, but its single-outlier spike has no cross-bitwidth gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint serves three roles: preventing catastrophic failure on spread architectures (Qwen: 32.45$\to$11.23), preventing moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: 8.85$\to$within 0.5\% of uniform), and rendering solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all tested architectures (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B spike) and a MHA architecture (Pythia-1.4B). Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen-7B's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

Non-uniform per-head KV cache quantization helps only when head sensitivity exhibits a specific distribution shape---a finding obscured by prior work's focus on aggregate metrics.
We study seven models spanning 1.4B--14B parameters and five architecture families (MHA through GQA 8:1) on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ and find that the benefit of per-head allocation depends not on GQA ratio or overall sensitivity magnitude, but on whether heterogeneity is \emph{spread} across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients or concentrated in a single outlier.
On the one spread-pattern model (Qwen2.5-7B), a cardinality-constrained solver achieves 11.23 perplexity at $4\times$ compression---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45)---while unconstrained solvers fail catastrophically (32--37 PPL) due to 2-bit distortion compounding through the residual stream.
On the remaining six models---including Qwen2.5-14B, where scaling dilutes spread into spike---non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit: Yi-1.5-9B has the highest concentration tested (0.71, exceeding Qwen-7B's 0.61) yet gains nothing, because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth gradient.
The cardinality constraint prevents catastrophic failure on spread architectures, moderate over-allocation on flat architectures (Gemma-2: unconstrained $1.47\times$ degradation reduced to within 0.5\% of uniform), and renders solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations---enabling a simple $O(H\log H)$ greedy algorithm.
We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including a within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B spike).

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across seven models at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 ($d_h(2){=}13.12$, second-ranked head: $0.55$, a $24\times$ gap; $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$, so upgrading it from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go---a ``spike'' pattern with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern enabling meaningful reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$), leaving no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.16 vs.\ $+$0.14 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

Pythia-1.4B extends the evaluation to MHA (1:1 ratio, 384 heads).
Despite low concentration ($0.24$), Pythia exhibits a spike pattern ($t_1/t_5{=}1.94$) with sensitivity in mid-layer heads (L1, L8--L17) rather than Layer-0, confirming that the spike/flat distinction generalizes beyond GQA architectures.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent concentration dilution.}
Qwen2.5-14B (GQA 5:1, 384 heads) provides a within-family comparison: concentration drops from 0.61 (7B) to 0.33 (14B), and $t_1/t_5$ rises from 0.57 to 24.35---a transition from spread to spike.
Sensitivity is dominated by a single head (L0H5, $d_h(2){=}1.845$; second-ranked: $0.237$, a $7.8\times$ gap), while the $3.4\times$ increase in head count ($112{\to}384$) dilutes the remaining signal below the concentration threshold.
Spread heterogeneity is thus not an intrinsic property of an architecture family but depends on scale: the diagnostic correctly identifies Qwen-7B as the single model$\times$scale combination where non-uniform allocation helps.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). --- = experiment pending. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok).}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Qwen2.5-14B & 5:1 & 0.33 & 24.35 & --- & --- & Spike \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.24 & 0.41 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^{*\dagger}$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.38 & $+$0.14 & $+$0.16 & Flat \\
Pythia-1.4B & 1:1 & 0.24 & 1.94 & --- & --- & Spike \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The per-head heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap}, Appendix~\ref{sec:heatmap_appendix}) confirms this visually: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero (spread); Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform (spike); Gemma-2 and Mistral show uniformly low distortion.

\subsection{Empirical Decision Rule}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint empirical decision rule for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile.
Given the profiling results from \S\ref{sec:profiling}, compute the top-5\% concentration and $t_1/t_5$ ratio, then select:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform recommended. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): $-$27.3\% PPL.
\item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. A single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient cannot be exploited. Yi-1.5 (0.71, 0.90), Llama (0.57, 0.85), Qwen-14B (0.33, 24.35), and Pythia (0.24, 1.94): no benefit.
\item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Too little cumulative delta for meaningful reallocation; $t_1/t_5$ is irrelevant. Mistral (0.24) and Gemma-2 (0.23): counterproductive.
\end{itemize}

Both conditions are needed: Llama's concentration (0.57) exceeds the 0.50 threshold but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no benefit.
A concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71, Llama at 0.57).
The rule correctly classifies all seven models (7/7), including the within-family scale contrast (Qwen-7B spread vs.\ 14B spike) and the MHA architecture (Pythia).
Only Qwen-7B exhibits the spread pattern ($N{=}1$); the suggested thresholds should be treated as illustrative until confirmed on additional spread architectures.
The rule reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no overhead.

Additional analyses---granularity tradeoff (Appendix~\ref{sec:granularity}), aggressive compression, profiling resolution and stability, per-layer optimality, and KV separation---are in Appendices~\ref{sec:granularity}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate seven models spanning five architecture families and diverse attention configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112),
\textbf{Qwen2.5-14B} (GQA 5:1, 48 $\times$ 8 = 384),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (GQA 8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (GQA 4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256, sliding window attention),
\textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (GQA 2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping),
and \textbf{Pythia-1.4B} (MHA 1:1, 24 $\times$ 16 = 384).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 1:1 (MHA) to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, softcapped, and multi-head attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
We use two profiling resolutions: \emph{standard} (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) and \emph{high-resolution} (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens), both from WikiText-2 train.
Unless marked with $\dagger$, all results use standard-resolution profiling; Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} analyzes the effect of resolution.

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen-7B, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2; Qwen-14B and Pythia $k$ values pending).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure severity tracks heterogeneity shape: catastrophic on Qwen-7B ($3.3\times$ bf16), moderate on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), mild on the remaining models (${\sim}1.1\times$). Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}; --- = experiment pending. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok). $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & Uncons. & Ours \\
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{11.23} \\
Qwen2.5-14B     & 5.84  & ---   & ---   & --- \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
Gemma-2-9B$^{*\dagger}$   & 6.03  & 6.17  & 8.85  & 6.20 \\
Pythia-1.4B     & 13.63 & ---   & ---   & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 11.23 PPL, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45); hires profiling further improves this to 10.91 (Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}).
Without the constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure from excessive 2-bit assignments compounding across layers.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%)---a genuine negative result, as the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity.

On Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) matches uniform at 7.22 PPL.
Despite the highest concentration tested (0.71), sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier (L4H3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern with no cross-bitwidth gradient to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B$^*$ (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 6.20 PPL vs.\ uniform 6.17, slightly above ($+$0.4\%).
Despite its flat sensitivity distribution (concentration 0.23), unconstrained MCKP degrades to 8.85 ($1.47\times$ bf16)---a moderate failure driven by the solver assigning 31.5\% of heads to 2-bit (vs.\ 4.7--16.4\% in other non-spread models).
The constraint reduces 2-bit heads from 106 to 8, confirming that it universally prevents over-allocation regardless of distribution shape.

Unconstrained failure severity tracks heterogeneity shape: catastrophic on Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), moderate on Gemma-2 ($1.47\times$), mild on the remaining three (${\sim}1.07$--$1.08\times$).
The allocation visualization (Figure~\ref{fig:allocation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:allocation_appendix}) and budget sweep (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget_sweep}) provide additional detail.

MCKP consistently outperforms random L0-constrained allocation and naive positional baselines across all three tested models (median gap 5--16\%; Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} in Appendix~\ref{sec:heuristic_appendix}).

\subsection{Downstream Evaluation}
\label{sec:downstream}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{0-shot accuracy change (Ours $-$ Uniform, pts) at 4$\times$ compression. Qwen shows large gains; the remaining models show small degradations or neutrality, tracking PPL results. $^\dagger$Hires profiling.}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & ARC-C & HS & PIQA & WG & Avg \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B        & $+$3.2 & $+$4.0 & $+$1.3 & $+$2.0 & $+$2.6 \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$        & $-$3.2 & $-$0.6 & $-$0.3 & $+$1.3 & $-$0.8 \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$     & $-$2.7 & $-$0.1 & $-$0.7 & $-$0.2 & $-$1.0 \\
Mistral-7B$^\dagger$       & $-$1.2 & $-$0.2 & $+$0.4 & $-$1.0 & $-$0.5 \\
Gemma-2-9B$^\dagger$       & $-$0.2 & $+$0.3 & $-$0.1 & $+$0.8 & $+$0.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On Qwen, constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 pts over uniform (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), recovering $\sim$73\% of the accuracy lost to quantization.
The four non-spread architectures show minor average degradation (Yi $-$0.8, Llama $-$1.0, Mistral $-$0.5, Gemma-2 $+$0.1 pts).
ARC-Challenge shows the largest per-task sensitivity across all models (Yi $-$3.2, Llama $-$2.7, Mistral $-$1.2, Gemma-2 $-$0.2 pts), consistent with multi-step reasoning where KV cache errors accumulate.
Cross-dataset stability analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:cross_dataset}) confirms ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement between WikiText-2 and C4 calibration across all three tested models.

content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_2/projects/ratekv/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — ratekv\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR submission)\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026 (11 days from today 2026-05-14)\\n- Track: Efficient Methods for NLP\\n\\n## bf16 Consistency Resolution (2026-05-14)\\n\\n**已解决**：qwen_bf16_reeval 确认 bf16 ≈ fp16（baseline delta=0.0006, uniform delta=0.005）。compounding_sweep bf16 rerun 不需要。\\n\\n**eval pipeline 一致性**：exp_e 使用了不同的 eval 参数（baseline=8.82, MCKP=9.57），与主 pipeline（baseline=9.81）不一致。hires_mckp_reeval 用统一 pipeline 重测：MCKP hires bf16=10.9131。**论文使用统一 pipeline 数字**。\\n\\n| 指标 | 统一 pipeline (bf16) | exp_e pipeline (bf16) | fp16 (旧) |\\n|------|---------------------|----------------------|-----------|\\n| Baseline | **9.8106** | 8.819 | 9.81 |\\n| Uniform 4-bit | **15.4454** | — | 15.45 |\\n| MCKP hires (max_2bit=8) | **10.9131** | 9.569 | — |\\n| MCKP lowres (max_2bit=8) | ~11.23 | 11.345 | 11.23 |\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nPer-head KV cache quantization sensitivity varies dramatically across architectures, and the effectiveness of non-uniform mixed-precision allocation is fundamentally determined by the degree of this heterogeneity. We provide both the analysis framework — characterizing when non-uniform quantization helps via per-head sensitivity concentration metrics — and a surprisingly simple method fix: a cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) that prevents compounding effects from profiler non-additivity and reduces the search space sufficiently that solver choice becomes irrelevant (greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations).\\n\\n## Core Claims (3 条)\\n\\n1. **Head sensitivity heterogeneity is architecture-dependent and determined by sensitivity *distribution shape*, not GQA ratio or concentration alone**: Per-KV-head quantization sensitivity is extremely non-uniform within models, but whether MCKP can exploit this heterogeneity depends on the *shape* of the sensitivity distribution, not just its magnitude. Critical counterexample: Yi-1.5-9B (GQA 8:1, concentration 0.71 — the *highest* in our lineup) provides *no benefit* from MCKP (7.22 vs 7.22 uniform), while Qwen2.5-7B (GQA 7:1, concentration 0.61) succeeds (+27.3%). The difference is distribution shape: Qwen has a *cluster* of sensitive heads (Layer 0, 4 heads with cross-bitwidth gradients — \\\"spread\\\" pattern, t₁/t₅=0.57), while Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier (L4H3, delta=13.12, t₁/t₅=0.90 — \\\"spike\\\" pattern) with sensitivity at only one bitwidth. A joint diagnostic — concentration ≳0.50 AND t₁/t₅ ≲0.70 — correctly separates the beneficial case (Qwen) from all four non-beneficial cases across five architectures. Three shape categories emerge:\\n   - **Spread** (Qwen): high concentration + low t₁/t₅ → multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients → MCKP effective\\n   - **Spike** (Yi-1.5, Llama): high t₁/t₅ → single outlier dominates → MCKP ineffective\\n   - **Flat** (Mistral, Gemma-2): low concentration → near-uniform sensitivity → MCKP ineffective (t₁/t₅ irrelevant when concentration < 0.50)\\n\\n2. **Cardinality constraint is the primary intervention; unconstrained catastrophe is Spread-specific**: On non-consecutive discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16}, unconstrained allocation produces **catastrophic** results on Spread-heterogeneity architectures (Qwen: greedy 32.45, MCKP 36.92 vs uniform 15.45 = 3.31× baseline) because per-head independent profiling distortions compound non-additively when many heads are simultaneously assigned extreme quantization. On non-Spread architectures, unconstrained allocation causes **mild-to-moderate degradation** (Yi 1.08×, Llama 1.07×, Mistral 1.08×, Gemma-2 1.47×) but still underperforms uniform 4-bit in all cases — the solver over-allocates 2-bit heads even when individual distortions appear small. A cardinality constraint (max_2bit≤k) is a simple and sufficient condition: it prevents compounding on Spread models, avoids 2-bit over-allocation on non-Spread models, AND reduces the feasible set to where solver choice is irrelevant — constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical bit allocations and PPL (Δ=0.0000, both 11.2312). **Practical implication**: the concentration diagnostic determines whether to invest in MCKP + constraint (Spread models) or simply use uniform 4-bit (non-Spread models — saves solver computation with no quality loss). The profiling benefit beyond the constraint (hires vs lowres) is architecture-dependent: substantial on Spread models (Qwen), marginal on others. The optimal k is determinable via small-scale compounding effect test (plan_004).\\n\\n**Claim 2 three-pillar support** (Reviewer Q4, new narrative STRENGTHENS Claim 2):\\n1. Spread models: constraint prevents catastrophe (Qwen 32.45→11.23)\\n2. Flat models: constraint prevents moderate over-allocation (Gemma-2 8.85→~6.17, 106→8 heads at 2-bit)\\n3. All models: constraint makes solver choice irrelevant (greedy=MCKP, Δ=0.0000)\\nThis answers \\\"when\\\" and \\\"why\\\", not just \\\"what\\\" — stronger than original \\\"universal catastrophe\\\" narrative.\\n\\n3. **A joint empirical decision rule correctly separates beneficial from non-beneficial architectures**: Constrained allocation achieves 27.3% PPL improvement on Qwen (spread pattern: concentration 0.61, t₁/t₅=0.57), while providing no benefit on Yi-1.5 (spike: 0.71, t₁/t₅=0.90, ≈0%), Llama (spike: 0.34, t₁/t₅=0.71, +0.2%), Mistral (flat: 0.22, t₁/t₅=0.18, -0.4%), and Gemma-2 (flat: 0.23, t₁/t₅=0.38, -0.3%). The joint condition — concentration ≳0.50 AND t₁/t₅ ≲0.70 — correctly separates the beneficial case from all four non-beneficial cases across five architectures (5/5 accuracy). Concentration alone fails: Yi-1.5 (0.71) exceeds Qwen (0.61) yet gains nothing, because its spike pattern (single outlier, no cross-bitwidth gradient) cannot be exploited. Under aggressive compression (≥5×), constrained allocation prevents catastrophic collapse even on non-beneficial architectures (Llama 5.3×: constrained PPL 57.60 vs uniform 2-bit 2644). This provides practitioners an empirical decision rule for when to invest in mixed-precision KV cache quantization. **Claim strength note (Reviewer-verified)**: N=1 Spread → position as \\\"empirical decision rule\\\", NOT \\\"diagnostic framework\\\". If Qwen2.5-14B also confirms Spread → upgrade to \\\"empirical diagnostic\\\" (N=2).\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: KV cache quantization typically applies uniform bit-width across all heads. Per-head mixed-precision allocation promises better quality-compression tradeoffs, but two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (1) *when* does non-uniform allocation actually help — i.e., under what architectural and compression conditions does the added complexity pay off? (2) *how* to make existing allocation algorithms (greedy, MCKP) work correctly on hardware-aligned discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16} where they currently fail catastrophically?\\n\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**: RateQuant (May 2026) provides R-D optimal per-head allocation via continuous closed-form (Theorem 2) and discrete greedy (Algorithm 1, optimal on consecutive integers {2,...,6} per Proposition 6). Moreover, unconstrained MCKP fares even worse (PPL 36.92) due to compounding effects from profiler non-additivity. Critically, neither RateQuant nor ARKV addresses *when* non-uniform allocation is beneficial.\\n\\n- **Our framing**: We present a systematic study of per-head KV cache quantization sensitivity across architectures and identify a surprisingly simple fix for the failure of existing algorithms on hardware-aligned bit-widths: a cardinality constraint limiting the number of heads assigned to extreme quantization levels. This single intervention (a) prevents compounding effects, (b) reduces the search space to where solver choice is irrelevant — greedy and MCKP produce identical optimal allocations, and (c) can be parameterized via a small-scale compounding test. Beyond the method, we establish that the benefit of non-uniform allocation is architecture-dependent and quantifiable via an empirical decision rule (concentration + distribution shape), providing practitioners a two-metric check for when mixed-precision is worthwhile.\\n\\n- **Headline result template**: \\\"We show that the benefit of non-uniform per-head KV cache quantization is concentration-dependent: on spread-heterogeneity architectures (Qwen, concentration 0.61), unconstrained solvers fail catastrophically (PPL 32-37 vs uniform 15.45), while a cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) achieves 27.3% PPL improvement with identical results from greedy and MCKP (Δ=0.0000). On non-spread architectures (4 models, 1.07-1.47× baseline), unconstrained solvers cause only mild degradation, and constrained MCKP offers no benefit over uniform 4-bit at either PPL or downstream task level (<1pp avg). An empirical decision rule (concentration ≳0.50 AND t₁/t₅ ≲0.70) correctly separates the beneficial case from all four non-beneficial cases (5/5 accuracy) at both PPL and downstream task level, providing practitioners a two-metric check to determine whether mixed-precision KV cache quantization is worthwhile — or whether uniform quantization suffices.\\\"\\n\\n## \\\"When Does Non-Uniform Allocation Help?\\\" — Analysis Chapter\\n\\nFive case studies representing the full spectrum of heterogeneity:\\n\\n| Case | Model | GQA | Top-5% Conc. | Constrained vs Uniform (4×) | Role in Paper |\\n|------|-------|-----|--------------|------------------------------|---------------|\\n| **Strong positive** | Qwen2.5-7B | 7:1 | 0.59-0.66 | **+27.3% (11.23 vs 15.45)** | Primary showcase; \\\"spread\\\" pattern (L0 cluster, 4 heads, 26× dominance) |\\n| **GQA counterexample** | Yi-1.5-9B | 8:1 | 0.71 (hires) | ≈0% (7.22 vs 7.22) | Highest GQA but no benefit; \\\"spike\\\" pattern (L4H3 single outlier, 34% of total delta) |\\n| **Marginal** | Llama-3.1-8B | 4:1 | 0.34-0.59 | +0.2% (8.45 vs 8.47) | Boundary condition; constraint never binds (natural k=2) |\\n| **Negative** | Mistral-7B-v0.3 | 4:1 | 0.22 (hires) | -0.4% (7.16 vs 7.13) | Profiler zero-signal; monotonic k-PPL curve |\\n| **Strongest negative** | Gemma-2-9B | 2:1 | 0.23 (hires) | -0.3% (9.05 vs 9.03) | Low-end anchor; most uniform sensitivity (CV=1.28, t₁/t₅=0.38) |\\n\\n**Spike vs Spread insight**: Yi-1.5 vs Qwen illustrates why GQA ratio alone is insufficient. Both have high GQA (8:1 vs 7:1), but Qwen's L0 *cluster* of sensitive heads creates optimization opportunities for MCKP, while Yi-1.5's single extreme outlier (L4H3) cannot be exploited — the solver assigns 8-bit to that one head but has no other heads to differentiate. Distribution shape matters more than the existence of outliers.\\n\\n**Compression amplifies benefit**: Even on low-heterogeneity Llama, aggressive 5.3× compression yields constrained PPL=57.60 vs uniform 2-bit=2643.77 (45× better).\\n\\n**Joint diagnostic** (n=5, 5/5 correct): concentration ≳0.50 AND t₁/t₅ ≲0.70 → non-uniform allocation recommended (spread pattern). Per-head KV cache quantization sensitivity varies dramatically across architectures, and the effectiveness of non-uniform mixed-precision allocation is fundamentally determined by the degree of this heterogeneity. We provide both the analysis framework — characterizing when non-uniform quantization helps via per-head sensitivity concentration metrics — and a surprisingly simple method fix: a cardinality constraint (≤k heads at 2-bit) that prevents compounding effects from profiler non-additivity and reduces the search space sufficiently that solver choice becomes irrelevant (greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations).

## Core Claims (3 条)

1. **Head sensitivity heterogeneity is architecture-dependent and determined by sensitivity *distribution shape*, not GQA ratio or concentration alone**: Per-KV-head quantization sensitivity is extremely non-uniform within models, but whether MCKP can exploit this heterogeneity depends on the *shape* of the sensitivity distribution, not just its magnitude. Critical counterexample: Yi-1.5-9B (GQA 8:1, concentration 0.71 — the *highest* in our lineup) provides *no benefit* from MCKP (7.22 vs 7.22 uniform), while Qwen2.5-7B (GQA 7:1, concentration 0.61) succeeds (+27.3%). The difference is distribution shape: Qwen has a *cluster* of sensitive heads (Layer 0, 4 heads with cross-bitwidth gradients — "spread" pattern, t₁/t₅=0.57), while Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier (L4H3, delta=13.12, t₁/t₅=0.90 — "spike" pattern) with sensitivity at only one bitwidth. A joint diagnostic — concentration ≳0.50 AND t₁/t₅ ≲0.70 — correctly separates the beneficial case (Qwen) from all four non-beneficial cases across five architectures. Three shape categories emerge:
   - **Spread** (Qwen): high concentration + low t₁/t₅ → multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients → MCKP effective
   - **Spike** (Yi-1.5, Llama): high t₁/t₅ → single outlier dominates → MCKP ineffective
   - **Flat** (Mistral, Gemma-2): low concentration → near-uniform sensitivity → MCKP ineffective (t₁/t₅ irrelevant when concentration < 0.50)

2. **Cardinality constraint is the primary intervention; unconstrained catastrophe is Spread-specific**: On non-consecutive discrete bit-widths {2,4,8,16}, unconstrained allocation produces **catastrophic** results on Spread-heterogeneity architectures (Qwen: greedy 32.45, MCKP 36.92 vs uniform 15.45 = 3.31× baseline) because per-head independent profiling distortions compound non-additively when many heads are simultaneously assigned extreme quantization. On non-Spread architectures, unconstrained allocation causes **mild-to-moderate degradation** (Yi 1.08×, Llama 1.07×, Mistral 1.08×, Gemma-2 1.47×) but still underperforms uniform 4-bit in all cases — the solver over-allocates 2-bit heads even when individual distortions appear small. A cardinality constraint (max_2bit≤k) is a simple and sufficient condition: it prevents compounding on Spread models, avoids 2-bit over-allocation on non-Spread models, AND reduces the feasible set to where solver choice is irrelevant — constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical bit allocations and PPL (Δ=0.0000, both 11.2312). **Practical implication**: the concentration diagnostic determines whether to invest in MCKP + constraint (Spread models) or simply use uniform 4-bit (non-Spread models — saves solver computation with no quality loss). The profiling benefit beyond the constraint (hires vs lowres) is architecture-dependent: substantial on Spread models (Qwen), marginal on others. 1. Spread models: constraint prevents catastrophe (Qwen 32.45→11.23)
2. Flat models: constraint prevents moderate over-allocation (Gemma-2 8.85→~6.17, 106→8 heads at 2-bit)
3. All models: constraint makes solver choice irrelevant (greedy=MCKP, Δ=0.0000)

3. **A joint empirical decision rule correctly separates beneficial from non-beneficial architectures**: Constrained allocation achieves 27.3% PPL improvement on Qwen (spread pattern: concentration 0.61, t₁/t₅=0.57), while providing no benefit on Yi-1.5 (spike: 0.71, t₁/t₅=0.90, ≈0%), Llama (spike: 0.34, t₁/t₅=0.71, +0.2%), Mistral (flat: 0.22, t₁/t₅=0.18, -0.4%), and Gemma-2 (flat: 0.23, t₁/t₅=0.38, -0.3%). ## Story Spine

- **Problem**: KV cache quantization typically applies uniform bit-width across all heads. Per-head mixed-precision allocation promises better quality-compression tradeoffs, but two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (1) *when* does non-uniform allocation actually help — i.e., under what architectural and compression conditions does the added complexity pay off? Critically, neither RateQuant nor ARKV addresses *when* non-uniform allocation is beneficial.

- **Our framing**: We present a systematic study of per-head KV cache quantization sensitivity across architectures and identify a surprisingly simple fix for the failure of existing algorithms on hardware-aligned bit-widths: a cardinality constraint limiting the number of heads assigned to extreme quantization levels.
